hook: So poached, conservationists engrave the shells.

story.text: The ploughshare tortoise carries a high golden dome of a shell, named for the plough-shaped horn that juts forward beneath its chin.
It survives nowhere but the dry bamboo-scrub of Baly Bay, northwestern Madagascar — a wild range of perhaps sixty square kilometers.
The shell that makes it beautiful made it a target: prized on the black market, owned as a status symbol.
Between 2002 and 2016, 334 ploughshare tortoises were seized from traffickers.
The wild population fell to a few hundred, then fewer; the Turtle Survival Alliance now presumes the species functionally extinct in the wild.
The defenses are extraordinary: conservationists engrave identification numbers into the shells to discourage poachers, and the breeding center works under armed guard.
That breeding center matters because Durrell cracked the code: the first captive breeding of the species, begun as Project Angonoka in 1986.
Over 800 captive-bred tortoises now live at Ampijoroa, and 105 have gone back to the wild.
Everything about the species is slow — maturity at fifteen years, three eggs to a clutch — so every tortoise counts.
To witness the ploughshare is to insist that a shell's beauty belong to the animal wearing it.

editorial.notes: Card v2 drafted from verified Durrell, Turtle Conservancy, TSA, and Chelonian Research Foundation pages. The CRF PDF is a 2008 assessment reprint hosted by CRF (not the IUCN API; the only rigorous source for size/clutch figures — flaggable under D-005 if AV wants it swapped). Engraving phrased as 'to discourage poachers' (the verified wording). Male gular jousting was unverifiable and excluded. Baly Bay is the published park; no precise localities are given.

reproduction.text: One to six eggs per clutch — three on average — in up to four clutches between January and May. About half hatch, and a hatchling will not breed for at least fifteen years.

insight.text: In 2025, tortoises rescued from smugglers back in 2010 produced 25 hatchlings in California — the first breeding success outside Madagascar.
